exercises.objective: Explain why naive reference-acceleration tracking is unstable.
exercises.prompt: Suppose you command $u=M(q)\ddot q^{\text{ref}}_t+F(q,\dot q)$ directly, using the reference trajectory's own acceleration with no correction term. Explain why small errors (numerical, modeling, or disturbance-induced) accumulate unboundedly over time, rather than the system settling back onto the reference.
hints: This command has no dependence on the *actual* current error $q^{\text{ref}}_t-q_t$ at all, it only knows the reference's own acceleration, not how far the real system has already drifted from it.

If a small error appears at some time step (e.g. from numerical integration, an unmodeled disturbance, or an approximation in $M,F$), nothing in this control law actively pulls the system back, the next command still just replays the reference acceleration, oblivious to the accumulated drift.

Errors from every previous step simply carry forward and compound, since there's no restoring force analogous to DYN-02's $K_p$ term. This is exactly why a feedback (error-correcting) term is essential, not optional, even when you know the dynamics and reference trajectory perfectly.

exercises.objective: Derive that PD-corrected trajectory tracking makes the position error obey DYN-02's PD equation exactly.
exercises.prompt: Using $\ddot q^*_t=\ddot q_t^{\text{ref}}+K_p(q_t^{\text{ref}}-q_t)+K_d(\dot q_t^{\text{ref}}-\dot q_t)$ and inverse dynamics $u=M(q)\ddot q_t^*+F(q,\dot q)$ (so forward dynamics gives $\ddot q=\ddot q_t^*$ exactly, the nonlinearity cancels), define the tracking error $e(t)=q^{\text{ref}}(t)-q(t)$. Derive the ODE satisfied by $e(t)$, and show it's exactly DYN-02's PD characteristic equation (with unit mass).
hints: Since $u=M\ddot q^*+F$ and forward dynamics is $\ddot q=M^{-1}(u-F)$, substituting gives $\ddot q = M^{-1}(M\ddot q^*+F-F) = \ddot q^*$ exactly: the actual acceleration equals the commanded desired acceleration, the nonlinear $M,F$ terms have cancelled completely.

So $\ddot q = \ddot q^{\text{ref}}+K_p(q^{\text{ref}}-q)+K_d(\dot q^{\text{ref}}-\dot q)$. Differentiate $e(t)=q^{\text{ref}}(t)-q(t)$ twice: $\dot e = \dot q^{\text{ref}}-\dot q$, $\ddot e = \ddot q^{\text{ref}}-\ddot q$.

Substitute $\ddot q$ from above: $\ddot e = \ddot q^{\text{ref}} - \big[\ddot q^{\text{ref}}+K_p(q^{\text{ref}}-q)+K_d(\dot q^{\text{ref}}-\dot q)\big] = -K_pe-K_d\dot e$, i.e. $\ddot e+K_d\dot e+K_pe=0$. This is *exactly* DYN-02's PD closed-loop ODE (with $m=1$, since inverse dynamics already absorbed the true mass matrix), confirming the error dynamics really do behave like a unit-mass point mass under PD control, regardless of how complicated the underlying robot's true $M(q),F(q,\dot q)$ are.

exercises.objective: Derive the task-space acceleration formula from the task-space velocity relation.
exercises.prompt: Starting from $\dot\phi(q(t)) = J(q(t))\dot q(t)$ (the task-space velocity relation), derive $\ddot\phi(q) = J\ddot q+\dot J\dot q$ using the product rule.
hints: $\dot\phi(q(t))=J(q(t))\dot q(t)$ is a product of two time-dependent quantities, $J(q(t))$ and $\dot q(t)$. Differentiate using the product rule: $\ddot\phi = \dfrac{d}{dt}[J(q(t))]\dot q(t) + J(q(t))\dfrac{d}{dt}[\dot q(t)]$.

The second term is immediate: $J(q(t))\ddot q(t) = J\ddot q$. The first term, $\frac{d}{dt}[J(q(t))]$, is exactly $\dot J$ (the total time-derivative of the Jacobian as the robot moves along $q(t)$), multiplied by $\dot q(t)$.

Combining: $\ddot\phi(q) = \dot J\dot q + J\ddot q$, i.e. $\ddot\phi(q)=J\ddot q+\dot J\dot q$. (Independently verified against a finite-difference computation on a 2-link arm while authoring this module.)
